subject: physics_2
question_text: What is meant by wattless component of current?

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. The book prints "wattles" for wattless (printed p40, twice) — corrected here. Physics hand-checked: average power = V I cos(angle between V and the current component); the I sin φ component sits at 90° to the voltage, cos 90° = 0, so it transfers zero average power — that component is the wattless current.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The meaning
lines: The current in an a.c. circuit is wattless
when the average power consumed is zero.
steps.margin_note: First mark. The word average must appear — instantaneous power is not zero.
steps.why: Wattless is a literal name — a current that consumes no watts. The definition must say AVERAGE power: the energy taken in one quarter cycle is returned in the next, so the average over a full cycle is zero.
common_mistakes: Saying the instantaneous power is zero. It is the AVERAGE power over a cycle that is zero.

recall.must_convey: That a current is wattless when the average power it consumes is zero.

steps.memory_tip: Wattless = no watts — the average power over a cycle is zero.

steps.label: The component I sin φ
lines: Let φ be the phase angle between the emf and
the current I. Resolve I into two parts:
I cos φ along the voltage and I sin φ at 90°
The part at 90° gives average power
So I sin φ is called the wattless current.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name I sin φ and say why it carries no power: cos 90° = 0.
steps.why: Average power is V I cos(angle between them). The I sin φ component sits at 90° to the voltage, and cos 90° = 0, so this component transfers no average power — that is the whole meaning of wattless.
common_mistakes: Calling I cos φ the wattless component. I cos φ carries the power; the wattless part is I sin φ.
Leaving out the reason. cos 90° = 0 is what makes the average power vanish.

recall.must_convey: That the component I sin φ, at 90° to the voltage, gives zero average power and is the wattless current.

steps.memory_tip: cos carries, sin sits idle: I cos φ carries the power, I sin φ is wattless.

insider_note: The book prints wattles — write wattless. The mark is in naming I sin φ and saying why it carries no power: cos 90° = 0.
